title: Quentin and the Inheritance
premise: Kestrel Coldharbour, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory makes them the industry's best lie detector, is hired by an elderly client named Ambrose Vane to prove that his own murder has not yet happened — a claim backed by a life policy taken out against a death dated three weeks in the future. As Kestrel investigates, they discover a pattern of 'pre-documented' deaths in Vane's family estate, each one executed exactly as written in sealed documents held by a private trust. The killer is Vane's own archivist, a man who has spent decades curating the family's records and now treats murder as a form of bookkeeping, correcting what he sees as errors in the family's history. Kestrel must use their perfect recall of every document they've read to trap him before the final entry — Vane's own death, scheduled for the winter solstice — is filed as fact.
about_author: Jonah Iversen is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent eleven years reading other people's worst days and started writing fiction to give those days better endings. They live in a coastal town where fog rolls in most mornings, which they insist is excellent for plotting.

chapters.title: The Client Who Paid for Nothing
chapters.summary: Kestrel Coldharbour's POV. A wealthy old man walks into their office with a retainer too large to refuse: prove his murder hasn't happened yet. He slides over a life insurance policy with a death date three weeks out — his own. Kestrel, unsettled but intrigued by the impossible paperwork, accepts. Emotional beat: cold professional curiosity masking a flicker of dread.

chapters.title: Coldharbour Rules
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with flashbacks to their first case. We learn how their photographic memory works — and how it isolates them; they can never forget a face, a lie, or a corpse. Establish their methodical ethics and their rule never to take cases about the future. Emotional beat: loneliness of a mind that keeps everything.

chapters.title: Vane House
chapters.summary: Kestrel visits the Vane estate, a decaying mansion run like an archive. Every room is catalogued; a staff archivist, Mr. Pell, maintains the family records with unsettling devotion. Ambrose shows Kestrel the sealed trust documents — including one describing his own death in precise detail. Emotional beat: creeping unease beneath genteel surfaces.

chapters.title: A Death Already Written
chapters.summary: Kestrel reads the pre-dated death record: cause, time, location, even the weather on the solstice. It matches no accident or illness — it describes murder, methodically. Kestrel checks the trust's history and finds four prior 'pre-documented' deaths across two generations, all ruled natural or accidental. Emotional beat: the thrill of a real mystery igniting.

chapters.title: Four Funerals, Filed Neatly
chapters.summary: Kestrel digs into the archive's older volumes, reconstructing the earlier deaths: a drowning, a fall, a fire, a quiet heart failure. Each was recorded before it occurred, each signed off by a different family member — all now dead. Only Ambrose remains of the original signatories. Emotional beat: dawning horror at the scale.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Smile
chapters.summary: Kestrel interviews Pell, probing for cracks. Pell answers everything perfectly — too perfectly — quoting dates and file numbers from memory that rivals Kestrel's own. For the first time, Kestrel meets someone whose recall might match theirs. Emotional beat: intellectual sparring laced with mutual recognition and suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Memory Keeps
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, night, insomnia. They mentally replay every document from Vane House and notice an anomaly: a page number out of sequence in the 1968 ledger, as if a page were removed and replaced. Someone has been editing the family's past. Emotional beat: obsessive focus sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary Problem
chapters.summary: Following the money, Kestrel finds that each pre-documented death redirected inheritance toward the trust itself — controlled, generation after generation, by whoever holds the archivist's post. Pell's position predates everyone's memory of who appointed him. Emotional beat: motive crystallizing; power corrupting through custodianship.

chapters.title: Ambrose Confesses Something
chapters.summary: Ambrose admits he signed the original documents as a young man, believing them a symbolic family ritual — until the deaths began matching. He suspects himself complicit and hired Kestrel partly to absolve him. His guilt is genuine, but his memory is failing, and Kestrel realizes the only reliable witness is deteriorating. Emotional beat: pity entangled with urgency.

chapters.title: First Attempt
chapters.summary: A brake line fails on Kestrel's car on the cliff road above the estate. They survive by seconds and recognize the scene: it matches a marginal note in the trust files they read days ago — a contingency for 'the investigator.' The killer anticipated them. Emotional beat: fear turning personal.

chapters.title: Reading the Killer's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Kestrel compares handwriting across decades of trust documents and finds the same hand throughout — the archivist's post has always been held by the same person, or someone trained to write identically. Pell is either immortal in the records or heir to a method. Emotional beat: revelation reframing everything.

chapters.title: The Understudy
chapters.summary: Kestrel locates Pell's predecessor's grave and interviews the retired village doctor who signed the old death certificates. The doctor, dying himself, confesses he falsified causes under pressure from 'the man who kept the books' — and that there have been two Pells, master and apprentice, indistinguishable. Emotional beat: the horror of institutionalized murder.

chapters.title: Solstice Minus Nine
chapters.summary: With nine days left, Kestrel requests the full trust inventory officially, forcing Pell to open the deep archive. Among the ledgers Kestrel glimpses a fifth pre-documented death — undated, unnamed, described only as 'the correction.' Emotional beat: ticking-clock tension tightening.

chapters.title: The Correction
chapters.summary: Kestrel deciphers the pattern: the fifth entry isn't Ambrose's death — that's the decoy in the public file. The correction targets someone who could expose the trust. Cross-referencing recent visitors, Kestrel realizes it describes them: cause, method, the cliff road. Their near-miss wasn't an attempt; it was a rehearsal. Emotional beat: icy terror and resolve.

chapters.title: Allegiances
chapters.summary: Kestrel confronts Ambrose with the truth; he offers to dissolve the trust publicly, but his lawyer — revealed to be on the trust's payroll — stalls. Kestrel can no longer tell who inside Vane House is protected, complicit, or next. Emotional beat: paranoia; allies becoming question marks.

chapters.title: The Page That Was Removed
chapters.summary: Kestrel finally identifies the missing 1968 page by reconstructing the ledger's binding marks: it names the original Pell's true identity and the trust's founding purpose — erasing a bastard line of the family from inheritance via staged deaths. The murders are corrections to a genealogy. Emotional beat: the theme landing — power rewriting memory itself.

chapters.title: Trap Design
chapters.summary: Kestrel sets a counter-trap: they plant a false document in the archive stating the missing page has been found and copied, then let their own habits — known to the killer through the case file — leak the location. To beat a killer who knows their methods, Kestrel must falsify their own patterns for the first time. Emotional beat: gambler's calm.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: The bait is taken — but not by Pell. A second archivist, the apprentice, surfaces to retrieve the page, revealing the master-apprentice structure and that the elder Pell intends the younger to inherit the 'post,' including Ambrose's death. Kestrel follows the apprentice into the deep archive after dark. Emotional beat: descent into the heart of the machine.

chapters.title: The Deep Archive
chapters.summary: Climax begins. In the vault beneath Vane House, Kestrel confronts both Pells amid a century of corrected lives. The elder Pell argues murder as stewardship — order over chaos, the archive over the people in it. When Ambrose arrives uninvited to face his own death record, the standoff fractures. Emotional beat: ideology versus humanity at knife's point.

chapters.title: Filed Under Winter
chapters.summary: Climax resolves. The elder Pell moves to execute the solstice entry early; Kestrel uses their perfect memory aloud — reciting the exact inconsistencies in the trust's own records — to turn the apprentice against the master, proving the elder planned to eventually 'correct' the apprentice too. The apprentice intervenes; the elder falls into the archive's own machinery. Emotional beat: catharsis through truth weaponized.

chapters.title: Amendments
chapters.summary: Aftermath. Police untangle decades of falsified deaths; Ambrose dissolves the trust and donates the archive to historians, choosing memory over control. The apprentice, spared, testifies. Kestrel declines credit, disturbed by how close they came to understanding the killer's logic. Emotional beat: weary justice, moral hangover.

chapters.title: What Kestrel Chose to Keep
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Kestrel's POV. Back in the office, Kestrel writes the report and deliberately leaves one detail out — not for the client, but because some things shouldn't be filed. They burn Ambrose's advance check stub and keep, instead, a blank page from the Vane ledger: unwritten, uncorrected. Emotional beat: quiet peace; memory redeemed by choice.
